activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: After about age 40, the lens of the eye loses flexibility and cannot focus up close as well, a condition called presbyopia that reading glasses correct.
story:
Grandma Fran arrived on Saturday with one suitcase and a bag of tomato seed packets she wanted to plant in Brooke's backyard. While Brooke's dad carried the suitcase inside, Grandma knelt by the garden bed, then held a seed packet out at arm's length, squinting at the tiny print. She dug through her purse, pulled out a pair of reading glasses, and settled them on her nose.

"You forgot your glasses before and you had to borrow Dad's," Brooke said, crouching beside her.

"I didn't forget. I lost them somewhere between my house and the airport." Grandma pulled a tomato seed from the packet and pressed it into the soil with her thumb. "These eyes turn forty and then some. They don't focus up close the way they used to."

Brooke filed that away. All week she watched for the pattern. At breakfast, Grandma held the cereal box far out and tilted her head. At the kitchen table, she borrowed Brooke's dad's glasses again and gave them back after a minute, rubbing the bridge of her nose. On Thursday, Brooke and her friends Maya and Lexie set up a lemonade stand by the garage, and when Grandma came out to help count the coins, she stacked the quarters by feel instead of reading the totals on their hand-drawn sign.

Lexie's dad, Mr. Gagnon, came over that evening to help burn the dead branches in the backyard fire pit. He checked the pile, kept the bucket of water close, and moved the kindling away from the flammable paint cans by the fence before he struck the match. Grandma stood near the pit, holding a stick, and when she leaned in to inspect the label on the citronella candle, she held it out straight in front of her again, arm's length, like always.

Brooke had a hypothesis. It wasn't about forgetfulness or fussiness. Something about eyes past about age forty made close-up focus go soft, and reading glasses fixed it. She'd also noticed that the hinge mechanism on her dad's spare glasses, the little screw-and-fold part, matched a broken pair she'd seen in the junk drawer. On Friday she dug through the drawer, found the hinge screw on the hall floor near the coat hooks, and marched into the backyard where Grandma was watering the tomatoes.

"I petitioned Dad to take us to the drugstore," Brooke said. "There's a spinning rack of reading glasses by the register. One dollar from my allowance for the screwdriver kit, and I can fix the old pair as backup too."

Grandma laughed and shut off the hose. "Did you figure out what's wrong with my eyes, detective?"

"It has a name," Brooke said. "Presbyopia. The cashier told me when Dad held the rack label at arm's length, same as you."

Grandana Fran picked up the watering can, tucked it under her arm, and steered Brooke toward the gate. "Then let's go pick out some rose-colored frames."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result and is worth reporting.
story:
Ava set the two rulers perpendicular to each other on the kitchen table, taped them into a cross, and checked her list one more time. Her science fair project was supposed to prove that bean seeds sprout faster when music plays for them, and for three days she had played her brother's playlist to one tray of seeds and left the other tray silent. It had become a ritual: water both trays, count the sprouts, write the numbers in her notebook.

The problem was the numbers. The silent tray had eleven sprouts. The music tray had four. Ava counted again, moving her pencil along each row of soil, and got the same answer. She sat back and stared at the notebook, wondering whether she had mixed up the labels, or watered one tray more than the other, or whether the speaker's warmth had dried out that soil. But she had checked everything twice, and the pattern stayed the same. Her hypothesis had simply turned out wrong.

Her phone buzzed. It was Kalen, who was testing whether his model bridge held more weight with thicker popsicle sticks. "Mine snapped at half the weight I predicted," he said, his voice tight. "The whole project is ruined. I can't present nothing. Maybe I'll just say I never finished."

Ava looked at her notebook again, at the two neat columns of numbers that refused to agree with her. "Wait," she said slowly. "You still have a result. You found out the thick sticks didn't help. Isn't that a real scientific result too, even though it shows your prediction was wrong?" She heard Kalen breathe on the other end. "Think about it," she went on, turning a page. "You tested something, you measured it, you learned something true. My seeds proved me wrong too, and I'm going to put that on my poster. A wrong prediction is still worth reporting."

There was a pause, and then Kalen laughed, a little shaky but real. "So my board says, 'Thicker sticks made the bridge weaker.' That sounds so strange."

"It sounds like science," Ava said. After they hung up, she opened her poster board and wrote her title in careful marker letters: What the Seeds Told Me. Then she uncapped the red marker and circled the number eleven.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, given on November 19, 1863, was about 272 words long and took roughly two minutes to deliver.
story:
Henry stood at the back of the drama camp rehearsal room, index card damp in his hand. Mr. Kerr had assigned everyone a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing, and Henry's card held exactly four words: dogs, space, grandpa, thanks. On the stage, Kaitlyn was already pacing through her speech about ocean plastic, gesturing like the waves themselves.

"Two minutes is nothing," Himmat muttered beside him, folding his arms. "You can't say anything important in two minutes. That's the whole controversy with this assignment. It's too short."

Henry didn't answer, because a thought had just caught him somewhere behind his ribs. He raised his hand anyway, out of turn, and the room went quiet. "Mr. Kerr, is it true that the Gettysburg Address was really short?"

Mr. Kerr smiled the way he did when a kid had stepped onto the right path by accident. "Go look it up during break," he said. "Tell us what you find."

At break, Henry and Himmat crowded the old laptop in the prop corner. The screen glowed in the dim room, and Henry could smell the dusty velvet of the stage curtains behind them. There it was. Abraham Lincoln gave the Gettysburg Address on November 19, 1863. It was about 272 words long, and it took roughly two minutes to deliver. Henry read it twice, and the second time a small shiver ran down his arms, the kind he got when a stage light snapped on.

"That's the same time we get," Himmat said slowly. "Two minutes. And people still remember it."

"Exactly the same," Henry said. He tested it out loud, reading the address at a normal pace while Himmat timed him, and it filled almost the whole two minutes, steady and unhurried. So the problem wasn't the time. The problem was whether each word could pull its own weight, could propel the whole speech forward. Henry thought of his agile little dog, Meg, leaping the creek fence, and he began to write his hook: the day Meg jumped.

When his turn came, he walked to the mark on the stage floor, felt the warm boards through his shoes, and looked at Kaitlyn in the second row. "The day Meg jumped the fence, she was airborne for less than two seconds," he said. "Here is what happened next."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file, called EXIF metadata.
story:
The afternoon light saturated the computer lab, and Alex kept one eye on Nimrit's post while pretending to research volcanoes. She had put up a photo of her new cat at midnight, and by lunch a stranger had commented, "Cute cat. Maple Row has the best porches." Nimrit had never typed her street name anywhere. That was the factor Alex couldn't stop turning over, because there were only two ways someone could know it: she'd told them, or the photo had told them for her.

He remembered that morning in Ms. Clarke's class, when they had hung their symmetrical snowflake posters along the window wall. Ms. Clarke had taken a picture of the display on her phone and said, "I'll put this on the class page so your families can see it." Nobody had thought anything of it then. Now Alex thought about it a lot.

At lunch he borrowed Nimrit's phone, sent himself the cat photo, and opened the file's details on the library computer. There it was: a small map with a pin sitting right on Maple Row. "Whoa," he said, and turned the screen toward Leonardo. "When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it writes the exact GPS coordinates into the file. It's called EXIF metadata." Leonardo leaned in, squinting at the pin as if it might blink first.

The stranger's account had no name, no picture, and followed exactly eleven people, all from their school. Alex scrolled the comments and found the same account asking a kid in Ms. Clarke's other class whether the blue house with the crooked fence was his. He copied the profile and showed it to Nimrit, whose jaw did a slow, symmetrical drop, one side matching the other. She deleted the post before she even finished saying a word.

Then Alex remembered his own photo of the volcano poster, the one he'd shared two weeks ago, and opened its details on his phone. The pin glowed quietly on his own street. "Turn off your location services," he told Leonardo, already tapping through his settings, and behind them the library printer hummed out somebody's homework.

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: All Canadian provinces have one-chamber legislatures, so a provincial bill passes only one house before the lieutenant governor gives royal assent.
story:
Sebastian had eleven minutes to fix his display before the judges at city hall came around the corner, and his diagram of how a bill becomes a law was wrong. He knew it was wrong because Felicity kept tapping the bottom edge of his poster with her pen.

"Count the boxes," she said. "You have the bill going through two houses, like the federal one on Katarina's poster. But ours is a provincial bill. Look at Katarina's."

Katarina held up her own poster across the table. Her bill passed through one chamber, then a box labelled royal assent, then it became law. Sebastian's poster showed the bill passing a second house after the first, which meant he had drawn four steps where there should have been two.

"That's why the judges kept asking me last year whether I'd confused the two," Sebastian said. He peeled off two of his paper boxes and stared at the gap they left. "Provincial bills only pass one chamber. Then the lieutenant governor gives royal assent."

"Say the whole thing so you remember it under pressure," Katarina said. She was checking the clock above the doorway, where the judges were still three tables away.

"All Canadian provinces have one-chamber legislatures, so a provincial bill passes only one house before the lieutenant governor gives royal assent," Sebastian said. He printed a fresh box, wrote "one chamber" on it, and glued it in place. Felicity handed him the marker for the royal assent box before he even asked. This was the part he liked about working with them: when they collaborated, nobody had to explain who would do what next.

Mr. Traoré, the librarian who had signed their permission forms, leaned over the table. "One of the judges asked me an ambiguous question earlier," he said quietly. "She wanted to know whether you three understood the difference between the federal and provincial routes, or whether you'd just copied one diagram. That could be the deciding factor in your score."

Sebastian straightened the poster and tested his idea one last time, tracing the path with his finger, one chamber, then royal assent, then law. No extra boxes, no detours. The judges reached their table just as he set down the marker.

"So," the tallest judge said, picking up a plastic cup from the prop table. "Pretend this cup is a bill about bike lanes. Walk me through it."

Sebastian picked up a second cup, set it in front of the first, and slid both across the table, one step, then royal assent.

"Law," he said.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: On drawing pencils, H is usually read as 'hardness' and B as 'blackness', so a 6B pencil makes darker, softer marks than a 4H.
story:
Alexis sat at the kitchen table with her sketchbook open to a portrait of Mr. Do, the neighbour who let her pick tomatoes from his garden every August. The drawing was supposed to be a gift, but the shading had gone wrong. The whole face looked ghostly, like a photocopy of a photocopy, and she could not figure out why. She had used the same technique that got her an A on last week's landscape.

Madison leaned over her shoulder, skeptical. "You pressed hard enough? It looks like you barely touched the paper."

"I pressed so hard my thumb hurts," Alexis said. She flipped the pencil over and stared at the letters on the end. 4H. Interesting. Yesterday, drawing the landscape, she had reached into the pencil box without looking, same as today. She dug through the tin and found the pencil she remembered grabbing, a 6B. "Hey, Madison. What do you think H stands for?"

"Happy? I don't know. Maybe you should ask your tutor, since you have one now."

"My math tutor would not know pencils." But Alexis wondered. She set a clean sheet on the table and made one long stroke with the 4H, then one beside it with the 6B, using exactly the same pressure. The 6B line came out dark and soft, almost velvet. The 4H line stayed pale and crisp, like a scratch. Same hand, same push, different letters. So the pencil itself had to be the hidden cause of the ghost face, not her technique.

She tried 2H next, then 2B, laying the stripes side by side like a test chart. The more the letter leaned toward B, the darker the mark. "B must be blackness," she said slowly, "and H must be hardness." That would explain everything. Her landscape had been made with the 6B by accident, and today she had grabbed the 4H and blamed herself instead of the pencil.

She erased the ghost shading and started over, working the shadow under Mr. Do's jaw with the 6B in light layers. Within twenty minutes the face had warmth and weight. Zain knocked on the door to return a colander, saw the drawing, and stopped in the doorway. "Whoa. Since when can you do that?"

"Since I stopped fighting the wrong pencil," Alexis said, and added one more soft stroke to the smile.

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: To solve a two-step equation such as 2x + 3 = 11, undo the adding first by subtracting 3, then undo the multiplying by dividing by 2, giving x = 4.
story:
The community centre smelled like chlorine from the pool downstairs and old carpet from the tutoring room upstairs, where Cameron sat glaring at his worksheet. Ms. Moose, who ran the homework club, had paired him with Everley because Everley's marks in math were the highest in grade seven. Cameron did not want a mentor. He wanted the last three problems on the page to stop existing.

"They keep coming out as fractions," he said, jabbing his pencil at problem four. "2x + 3 = 11. I divide by two first, so x plus three equals five and a half, and then it just gets worse from there." He tried to compress the numbers into something smaller by erasing hard, but the paper only thinned and went grey.

Everley pulled the sheet toward her and tilted her head. "My brother did that for a month. Try the other order. Take away the three first."

"Take away the three," Cameron repeated slowly. Eleven minus three was eight. Then he divided by two, because the multiplying had been done last, so it got undone... he stopped and just wrote it. 2x = 8. x = 4. No fractions. He checked it backward: two times four was eight, plus three was eleven. His ears went warm. "Okay. Okay, that works."

The back of the sheet had a coordinate grid, and the last problem asked for the line that matched y = 2x + 3. Cameron plotted x = 4, found y = 11, and marked the point. He picked x = 0, got y = 3, marked that too, then x = 2 and y = 7. He laid his ruler flat through the dots and drew. The line ran clean and diagonal across the grid, and every point he tested landed on it exactly.

"You erased a hole in problem two," Everley said.

Cameron grinned and covered it with his hand. "It's fine. The paper's resilient."

"It's not," said Ms. Moose from the doorway, holding out a fresh sheet. "You are. Take another copy."

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Puberty is driven by hormones: the pituitary gland in the brain signals the ovaries or testes to make more estrogen or testosterone.
story:
Charlie stood in the bathroom with her arm raised like she was answering a question in class, sniffing cautiously at her own armpit. It had been fine yesterday. She had showered yesterday. So why, she wondered, did she smell like a wet dog wearing a gym sock?

"Did you die in there?" her brother called through the door. "Some of us need the mirror."

"One minute." She grabbed the deodorant stick her mom had left on the shelf, studied it like a suspect, and put it back down. Deodorant felt like admitting defeat. If she could just figure out the cause, she could fix the cause, and then she wouldn't need a stick of lavender wax rubbing itself on her every morning. That was how problems worked, wasn't it? Find the cause, remove it, victory.

Talya came over after lunch, and the two of them sat on Charlie's bed with the laptop and a stack of pamphlets her mom had brought home from the clinic. Charlie held up the top one. "This is for my brother," she said, "but I borrowed it. For science."

"For smell science," Talya said solemnly.

They read side by side, Talya's finger running parallel to Charlie's down the page, nearly colliding twice. Then Charlie stopped and read a sentence out loud. "Puberty is driven by hormones. The pituitary gland in the brain signals the ovaries or testes to make more estrogen or testosterone." She frowned. "So the smell isn't me being bad at showering. It's my brain sending a message."

"Your brain is tattling on you," Talya said. "Your own brain. Rude."

Charlie thought about it. She couldn't see the pituitary gland, couldn't feel it doing anything, but here was the proof, right under her nose, twice a day after gym. The message had already been sent. You couldn't unsend a message from your own brain, which she told Talya was basically a revolution in how she'd been thinking about the whole thing, and Talya said it was maybe a small revolution, and Charlie said revolutions start small, and they argued happily about the correct size of revolutions for a while.

The next morning Charlie ran a test. She showered, used the deodorant, and then tried to simulate a whole gym class in her bedroom, doing jumping jacks until her brother banged on the wall and told her the ceiling lamp was swinging. She sniffed. Lavender. Nothing else. Not a single wet dog, not one gym sock. The system worked.

She stuck the deodorant in her backpack next to her math book, where it would be ready every day, and wrote a note in marker on her hand as a backup: ASK MOM FOR A SECOND STICK FOR GYM BAG. Then she went down to breakfast, waving her arms like a champion crossing a finish line, and announced, "I smell incredible."

activity: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
knowledge_domain: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
fact: Guido van Rossum began creating Python in December 1989 and first published its code in February 1991.
story:
Tristan's times table program had been dormant on his screen for ten minutes. The cursor blinked after line three, and every time he imagined typing the next line, his fingers stopped. He wanted the program to print the times table for any number the user typed, because Mr. Saleh had promised that whoever got it working first could demo it on the projector at the coding club showcase on Friday.

Haris leaned over from the next computer. "You're stuck too?"

"Every time I try to write it, I end up printing the same line twelve times," Tristan said. "I don't want twelve lines. I want the loop to count."

"That's the part nobody taught us," Haris said. He scrutinized Tristan's screen, frowning at the three lines as if one of them might confess. "Leonard figured his out. Ask him."

Leonard was across the lab, already running his program, his screen scrolling with neat rows of numbers. Tristan walked over and watched. Leonard had typed a word Tristan hadn't used yet: for. One line, and the loop counted from 1 to 12 all by itself. Tristan went back to his seat and tried it. He typed "for i in range(1, 13):" and underneath it, "print(number, "x", i, "=", number * i)". When he ran it and typed 7, twelve lines rolled up the screen, seven times one all the way to seven times twelve.

"Ha!" said Haris, who had copied the idea and got his working a minute later.

Mr. Saleh came around checking screens. "For loops," he said. "The heart of Python. People forget how old that language is. Guido van Rossum began creating it in December 1989, and he first published its code in February 1991."

Tristan did the math in his head. Python was older than he was, older than everyone in the room, and it had been counting in loops since before any of them could type. He saved his file twice, once on the school drive and once on his flash drive, then raised his hand.

"Mr. Saleh. Can I try mine with a nine-digit number on the projector?"

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: Stage fright is the body's fight-or-flight response: adrenaline can cause a racing heart, a dry mouth, a shaky voice and trembling hands.
story:
Hayden stood in the wings of the community theater, clutching his song sheet so hard the paper crumpled. The red curtains smelled like dust and old paint, and the stage lights generated a warm glow that reached even backstage. In two songs, he would sing in front of three hundred people for the very first time. Then he looked down at his hands. They were trembling, fast, like a phone buzzing on a table.

His heart was pounding too, and when he swallowed, his mouth felt as dry as the chalk dust in Mr. Holloway's classroom. "Great," he whispered. "Now my voice will shake and everyone will hear it." Nelly peeked over his shoulder, following his stare at his own fingers. "That happens to everybody," she said. "It's fight-or-flight. Adrenaline, from being scared." She tapped a poster taped to the wall, a wrinkled one from last year's winter concert, with that same phrase printed on it in bold letters.

Hayden read the poster twice. Adrenaline could cause a racing heart, a dry mouth, a shaky voice, and trembling hands. Every single thing on that list was happening to him right now. So that was it. His body wasn't breaking; it was doing exactly what scared bodies did. He tested an idea: if the shaking was just extra energy coursing through him, maybe he could burn some of it off. He jogged in place behind the curtain rack, quick little steps, then shook out his arms like a swimmer before a race. Nelly raised an eyebrow. "You look like a confused flamingo." "A calm flamingo," Hayden said, and realized his hands had gone almost still.

Then came the twist. Helena marched past them toward the microphone for her solo, spine straight, chin up, every inch the confident lead. But as she passed, Hayden saw her hands. They were shaking so hard her cue cards rattled like a rattlesnake. He grabbed a water bottle from the prop table and pressed it into her fingers. "Dry mouth?" he asked. She nodded, biting her lip. "Drink this. Then shake your arms out, fast. It worked for me." Helena had wanted this solo since September, had practiced it in the stairwell every single lunch break, and now her whole dream was balanced on two trembling hands.

She gulped the water, flapped her arms like a bird about to take flight, and rolled her shoulders. Her cue music started. Helena walked out into the light, and Hayden held his breath. The first line came out clear and steady, and the second line was even stronger. Backstage, Nelly gripped Hayden's sleeve. "Two songs until we're on," she whispered. Hayden bounced on his toes, feeling his heart drum, not with fear now but with something a whole lot closer to joy. "Best idea I've ever tested," he said, and stepped toward the lights.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Puberty usually begins between ages 8 and 13 in girls and between 9 and 14 in boys, and starting anywhere in that range is normal.
story:
Cole sat in the waiting room of the doctor's office with his arms crossed, because Kelly-Anne from his class was sitting three chairs away and he did not want her to know why he was there. Too late. "Cole?" she said. "Is this about the smell thing?"

"There's no smell thing," he said, but the paper bag in his lap, which held every deodorant from the pharmacy shelf, disagreed with him. His mom had dumped all six on the counter and told the cashier, "Whichever one is most durable, please. He plays outside like a raccoon." Kelly-Anne was only there for her little brother's checkup, but she scooted over anyway and looked at the bag without laughing, which he appreciated.

In the exam room, Ms. Sow, who turned out to be the doctor and also the neighbor who grew tomatoes, sat down and let him go first. "Everyone in my class already got taller and I'm exactly the same as September," Cole said. "And also there's the smell thing. Am I broken?" He had a theory, actually. He'd been working on it for a week: the armpit bacteria that made the stink were tiny carnivores, and they were eating something, so if he could starve them out with the strongest deodorant, maybe his body would get the message and hurry up the growing part too. He explained this to Ms. Sow, and she wrote something down, which worried him until he saw it was a smiley face.

"Nobody's broken," she said. "Puberty usually begins between ages eight and thirteen in girls and between nine and fourteen in boys, and starting anywhere in that range is normal." She let that sit for a second. "So if you started at eleven, twelve, thirteen, even fourteen, all normal." Cole did the math in his head, then did it again because it felt too easy. Kelly-Anne's class had a chart on the wall from a science project, and half the boys had marked their growth spurts already, and he had been counting himself late. But if the whole range ran to fourteen, half the boys in his grade weren't ahead of him at all. They were just loud about it. He tested it out loud: "So the kids who grew first aren't winning anything. There's no race." Ms. Sow nodded.

"About the bacteria," she added, "daily showers and deodorant take care of it. You don't have to intimidate them." On the way out, Cole stopped at Kelly-Anne's chair and held out the bag. "Take the green one," he said. "It's a backup for Elie, since he won't admit anything." Kelly-Anne took it and said, "Tell him it's deodorant for carnivores."

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: A proposed law is called a bill until it passes all its stages; once it becomes law it is called an Act.
story:
Luke had been the one who suggested the field trip to city hall, back when Mr. Patel asked the class council for ideas. He wasn't so sure now. The chamber where the legislature met was almost empty on a Tuesday morning, rows of green benches gleaming under the lights, and a woman at the front desk had told them the members were in committee rooms upstairs.

"Don't touch the brass rail," Lillian whispered, though Luke hadn't been going to. He was staring at a display case instead. Inside it sat two documents under glass. One was labeled The Bicycle Helmet Bill. The one beside it was labeled The Bicycle Helmet Act.

"That's weird," Luke said. "Same law, two different names. Which one is it?"

Priya leaned in beside him. "Maybe one of them is fake."

Luke thought about the streetcar they had ridden that morning, how the conductor had punched each ticket twice, once at the front door and once at the back, and how at first he'd thought she was being careless. Then he'd realized the two punches meant two different things, checked on and checked off. Two names could mean two different things, too. He needed to test it.

He looked closer at the papers in the case. The bill had a stamp across the corner: FIRST READING, and further down, SECOND READING POSTPONED, then a date, then more readings after that. The Act had no readings at all. It had a big seal and a signature at the bottom.

"The bill one has stages," he said slowly. "First reading, second reading, third reading. The Act one just... is."

"So the names aren't the same thing wearing two hats," Priya said.

"A proposed law is called a bill until it passes all its stages," the woman at the desk said, walking past with a stack of folders. "Once it becomes law, it's called an Act." She kept going before Luke could ask anything else.

"It was a bill first," Luke said. "Then it finished, and it got a new name. Like how the ticket changed after the second punch."

Lillian frowned at the case. "That's going to be confusing forever, though. Two names for one thing."

"It's not one thing," Luke said. "That's the point."

They found Mr. Patel by the public gallery, where a plaque promised an impartial view of proceedings from the seats above. He asked Luke what he had learned, and Luke started to explain, then stopped, because upstairs a door banged open and a clerk called out that the committee had finished early and the chamber would sit in ten minutes after all.

"Sit!" Priya grabbed his sleeve. "We can actually watch."

They scrambled up to the gallery rail as members filed in below, and Luke leaned forward, listening for the word.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Squeezing or popping pimples can push bacteria deeper into the skin and can leave scars.
story:
Aaron sat in the waiting room of Dr. Patel's office, pressing his sleeve against the red lump on his chin every time someone looked his way. Rose and Abigael would be at Marcus's birthday party on Saturday, and the pimple had appeared on Wednesday like an alarm going off. His plan was simple: tonight, before the party, he would squeeze the thing until it was gone.

"Aaron Murray," the nurse called, and he followed her down the hall. Mr. He, his neighbour, was already in the exam room, waiting for his own follow-up appointment, and the nurse said they could share the room since Dr. Patel was running behind. Mr. He nodded at him. "That chin looks like it's bothering you," he said. "My son used to fuss over those."

Aaron said nothing. He had a question locked in his head, and he was not going to ask it in front of his neighbour.

But the room was small, and the clock ticked, and Aaron's fingers kept drifting up to his chin like they were testing something. Finally he said, "If you squeeze them, do they go away faster?"

Mr. He tilted his head. "You know what an acute problem is? Sharp, sudden, hits fast?" Aaron nodded slowly. "A pimple feels like that, but popping it doesn't solve it. Squeezing or popping pimples can push bacteria deeper into the skin, and it can leave scars."

Aaron's hand dropped from his chin. Scars. He pictured his face in ten years, with a little dent where the pimple had been, telling people about a birthday party in seventh grade. "So how long does it take if you leave it alone?" he asked.

"Days, sometimes. Your body handles it." Dr. Patel came in then, checked Mr. He's shoulder, and glanced at Aaron. "Here for the sports physical," she said, reading her chart. She looked him over, listened to his breathing, and then said, "While you're growing, your sweat glands are more active, and the oil in your skin changes too. Daily showers, and deodorant every morning. That's the adaptation most boys your age need to make."

"An adaptation," Aaron repeated. Like adjusting to a new rule nobody had told him about.

He walked home testing the idea. If he left the pimple alone and started showering every day instead of every other day, maybe fewer of them would show up. It was a pattern he couldn't see directly, but he could try it and find out. That night he showered, put on the new deodorant his mom had left on the counter, and left the pimple untouched, even though it itched like a mosquito bite he wasn't allowed to scratch.

At the party on Saturday, Rose squinted at his chin. "What happened to your face?"

"Nothing," Aaron said. "That's the point."

Abigael laughed. Then Marcus's mom brought out the cake, and Aaron, forgetting his chin completely, got in line for the biggest slice.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Estimating first catches mistakes: one half plus one third must be more than one half but less than one whole.
story:
The problem started the moment Mr. Guo wrote one half plus one third on the board and told the class to find the answer with unlike denominators. Abigail copied the problem into her notebook and stared at it. The two fractions looked like they belonged to different families, and she could not see how to make them match.

At home that evening, her little brother was hunched over the same kind of homework. He showed her his answer to one half plus one third: six fifths. "It's bigger than one," he said proudly. Abigail almost let it go, but something nagged at her. She thought about a chocolate bar. Half a bar plus a third of a bar had to be more than half a bar, sure, but less than a whole one. There was simply not enough chocolate there to cover a whole bar. Her brother's answer was too big, and she knew it before she did any math at all.

"Where did you get six fifths?" she asked.

He pointed at his work. He had added the tops and the bottoms separately, like they were ordinary numbers. She tried his method herself on paper, just to simulate what a person would get if the trick worked everywhere. One half plus one third gave him five fifths on her page too, and one third plus one half gave five fifths as well, which was strange, because those two problems should match, and five fifths made exactly one. But her chocolate picture said the real answer should sit between one half and one whole. The add-everything trick failed her test.

She remembered the day before, when Faith had split a sandwich with her at lunch. Faith had cut her half into three equal strips and said each strip was a sixth of the whole sandwich, which meant a third of a half was a sixth. Abigail wondered if that cutting idea could work here too. If she cut both halves and thirds into the same size pieces, the fractions might finally speak the same language. She tried sixths, because halves could become three sixths and thirds could become two sixths. Three sixths plus two sixths made five sixths. More than one half, less than one whole. Her estimate said yes.

The next morning she found Jayke by the lockers and showed him both answers side by side. "Critique my brother's method," she said, holding up the page. "Add the tops, add the bottoms. Six fifths."

Jayke frowned at it. "But a half plus a third can't be more than a whole. That's like claiming two slices of pizza are bigger than the entire pizza."

"Exactly," Abigail said. "Five sixths. The estimate catches it every time."

In class, Mr. Guo asked for a volunteer to solve the problem on the board. Abigail's hand went up before she decided to raise it. She wrote three sixths plus two sixths equals five sixths, then drew a quick bar divided into six pieces, shading five of them, a nutritious snack for the brain if there ever was one, Jayke whispered from the second row. Mr. Guo nodded and asked the class if anyone could explain why the answer had to be less than one whole.

"Because half a chocolate bar plus a third of a chocolate bar," Abigail said, "still leaves some chocolate bar missing."

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: Other signs of anxiety can include irritability, trouble concentrating, restlessness and asking again and again for reassurance.
story:
Ethan sat in the dentist's waiting room, flipping through a magazine about volcanoes, when his phone buzzed again. It was Clement, the fifth text in a row, all asking the same question: "u sure it doesn't hurt?" Ethan typed back "yes" the first time, "YES" the second, and after that he just stared at the screen. He counted the messages. Five. He remembered last week, when Clement had snapped at George over a lost pencil and then couldn't focus on the group project at all, bouncing his leg under the table the whole class. Ethan had mediated that argument without thinking twice, but this felt different, like pieces of a pattern he was only starting to see. Irritable. Distracted. Restless. And now asking again and again if things were okay.

The flashback hit him quick and sharp. Two weeks ago, Clement had come with him to this same office, sat beside him in the chair by the window, and talked nonstop so Ethan wouldn't think about the drill. Ethan had told him, laughing through dry lips, that his fear of dentists should have been extinct ages ago, like the dinosaurs in the volcano magazine. Clement had laughed too, but not really. His eyes had gone tight and small.

Now the irony landed on Ethan like a dropped book. He had been the scared one, the one everybody worried about, and the whole time Clement had been carrying the fear home with him, feeding it, texting it back to Ethan in loops.

Ms. Shapiro, their neighbour from two doors down, worked at the front desk here. Ethan walked over and showed her his phone, the five messages stacked like stairs. "I think he's really worried," Ethan said. "Not just normal worried. He keeps needing to hear it's fine." Ms. Shapiro read the screen, then looked at Ethan over her glasses. "You did the right thing bringing this to me instead of just answering again," she said. "Want to call him from the back room? It's quiet there."

Clement picked up on the second ring. "You're okay?" he asked before Ethan even said hello. "Completely fine," Ethan said. "It didn't hurt. And listen, next time you feel like this, you can tell somebody. You told me about your worry a hundred times without telling me at all." There was a long pause, then a shaky laugh on the other end. "That's the worst magic trick ever," Clement said. "Come over after," Ethan said, and hung up, still holding the volcano magazine against his chest.

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: Most modern tuning sets the A above middle C at 440 vibrations per second, or 440 hertz.
story:
William's part kept sliding into Klara's part like a magnet pulling a paperclip. Mr. Crowchild played an A on the piano, the note choirs everywhere use to find their starting pitch, and the two sections began again. Within four bars, William was singing the melody right along with the sopranos instead of holding the lower line.

"It's not your ears," Klara whispered afterward. "It's your brain. It wants to agree with us."

"That's ridiculous," William said, but that night he remembered second grade, when he and Channing had tried to whisper different secrets to each other at the same time and both ended up saying the same word, "pickles," for no reason. Brains did like to copy. Maybe his was doing it with sound.

The next morning he asked Channing to help him test the idea. Channing, who badly wanted the boys' section to beat the girls' at the spring concert, agreed at once. They faced each other in the music room before class. William sang a held note while Channing sang a different one, and William concentrated on feeling his own sound as a separate thing, like holding his side of a rope in a tug-of-war. When he stopped opposing Channing's note with his attention and just let it sit there in the background, his own pitch stopped wandering.

"See?" Channing said. "Logic. You can't fight the other part, you just have to not care about it."

At rehearsal, Mr. Crowchild struck the A again. "Remember," he said, "that note is the A above middle C, tuned to 440 vibrations per second. 440 hertz. Some of you find that fascinating."

"Actually," William said, "it kind of is."

Mr. Crowchild raised both eyebrows, clearly revising his opinion of William on the spot. The choir sang. William's line held, Klara's soared above it, and Channing grinned like a man winning a contest nobody else knew about.

"Two more from the top," said Mr. Crowchild, "and William, pretend the melody insulted your dog."

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: A swimmer's head pushes a bow wave that leaves a dip in the water beside the face, letting the mouth reach air below the level of the flat surface.
story:
Zoey sat in the dugout after baseball practice, still dusty from third base, reading the note her friend Allie had stuffed into her cleat bag.

"Dear Zoey," the note said. "My mom says the pond by the diamond is calm all week, so if you're going to pass your swim test on Saturday, that's the place to practice. Twenty-five metres front crawl, side breathing, no stopping. You can do this. P.S. I'll be at the game Saturday, so I can't come help, but Tiffany can. P.P.S. Bring the good googles."

The pond lay just past the outfield fence, flat and green in the evening light. Tiffany was already there, dragging a foam noodle through the water like a giant straw. "Coach says your arms look great," Tiffany called. "Like pistons. It's the breathing that's going to sink you."

Zoey waded in and tried a length. She managed four strokes, then lifted her whole face up, spluttered, and stood. Twice more, same thing. On the fourth try she noticed something strange. When she turned her head sideways, she didn't have to lift it as high as she thought. Right beside her cheek the water seemed to dip away, leaving a small pocket of air lower than the flat surface around it. She stopped and stared at the spot where her head had been. Her own head was pushing water ahead of it, and that pushed water left a hollow beside her face. She didn't need to climb for the surface at all. The dip did the work.

"That's controversial," Tiffany said when Zoey explained it, floating on her back. "I always lift way up. Everyone on the team lifts way up."

"Try it," Zoey said. "Turn your head slow and let the water make the pocket."

Tiffany tried it, got a mouthful of pond, and came up laughing. Then she tried again, slower, and it worked. "Okay," she said, wiping her eyes. "I change my mind. Don't tell Allie I ever doubted you, or she'll accuse me of being a terrible coach." They swam laps until the sun went orange behind the backstop, counting strokes out loud, fourteen and a breath, fourteen and a breath.

On Saturday morning Zoey stood at the pond edge, towel over her shoulder, and pointed herself at a maple tree on the far bank, twenty-five metres away. She pushed off, arms turning like pistons, and each time she rolled her head sideways the little dip opened beside her face and the air was right there, waiting. She touched the far bank, spun around, and shouted across the water, "I made it! One length, no stopping!" Tiffany, sitting on the dock with her cleats already on for the game, pumped her fist and yelled back, "Two out of three?"

activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
knowledge_domain: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
fact: A Bharatanatyam dancer's first full solo performance is called an arangetram, meaning ascending the stage, and marks the end of their first formal training.
story:
Katherine's feet kept landing half a beat late. In the temple hall, between the donation box and the smell of jasmine garlands, she practiced the same eight counts of adavus over and over while her cousin Priya watched from a folding chair.

"You're counting from your mouth," Priya said. "Count from your center."

Katherine stopped. She had been saying tha-ka-dhi-mi under her breath, and somehow the words were arriving before her feet. Maybe the problem was not her feet at all. Maybe the sound and the step were proportional, one always slightly ahead, like a shadow that moves a moment after you do. She tried an experiment: she hummed nothing at all and let her hand tap the beat against her ribs instead. The steps snapped into place.

"That's it!" Priya stood up. "See, you can't fix what you can't see. You had to find the hidden lag first."

At the next practice, Brenna and Chantelle came to watch, because Ms. Saleh had asked them to help plan the community gathering where Katherine would perform a short piece. Chantelle sat cross-legged on the floor, copying a hand gesture and getting it backwards.

"Your cousin's arangetram was amazing," Brenna said. "Two hours, all those songs."

"Arangetram," Priya said. "It means ascending the stage."

"It's after the first full training," Katherine added. "A dancer's first solo performance alone, the whole evening." She was still a long way from that. She had maybe four minutes of one piece, and the wobble in her turn that came back whenever she got nervous.

On the day of the gathering, the hall filled with aunties and uncles and kids from school. Katherine waited behind the curtain in her borrowed costume, ears buzzing. Then she remembered the hidden lag, pressed her palm flat against her ribs, and felt the beat travel down through her body like water finding a level. The drums began.

She stepped out, and her feet knew exactly what to do.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Relationship researcher John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which is about one specific action, from criticism, which attacks a person's character with words like 'you always' or 'you never'.
story:
Rebecca had the hull of their model sailboat half sanded when Anaelle's text arrived, and she almost knocked the whole thing off her desk. "Can I come over?" it said, which was wild, because they hadn't spoken since Friday. On Friday, Rebecca had told Anaelle a secret in confidence, and by Saturday the whole class knew. Rebecca had fired back one furious message: "You never keep secrets. You're just a blabbermouth." Anaelle hadn't replied at all.

Now Rebecca stood at her window watching for Anaelle's bike, her mind racing. Why had her own message felt so much worse than the thing she was actually mad about? She grabbed a notebook and wrote two lines. The first was what she'd sent: "You never keep secrets." The second was just the facts: "You told Oceane what I said on Friday." The second one, she realized, was only about one specific action. The first one attacked Anaelle herself, with "you never," like it was her whole character that was broken. She'd read somewhere that a researcher named Gottman called these two different things, but until now she hadn't really got it. A complaint was about one action. Criticism went after the person.

The doorbell rang. Rebecca took a huge breath and opened the door with the notebook still in her hand.

"I'm not a blabbermouth," Anaelle said before Rebecca could speak. "I made one mistake."

"I know," Rebecca said, holding up the notebook. "That's what I need to say. It was criticism, not a complaint. What I should have said was, you told Oceane what I said on Friday. That's it. That's the whole complaint."

Anaelle blinked, then read the two lines upside down. "The second one's easier to hear," she admitted. "Even though it's about the same thing."

"That's the rule, I think," Rebecca said. "One action, not the whole person. Also, Oceane told me you didn't even mean to tell her. You were doing impressions and it slipped out."

Anaelle groaned. "It was an exceptional impression of Mr. Joshi. I couldn't stop it."

"Show me," Rebecca said, pulling her toward the desk where the hull waited, half sanded, ready for both of them. "Then we finish the boat before dinner, and this time I'm only telling you fake secrets, as a test."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977: the tendency to blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation.
story:
Victoria stared at the group chat on her phone. Three names sat at the top of the screen: her, Hanna, and Hassan. Their science project was due Friday, and Hassan had answered every question with one flat word. "Fine." "Later." "Whatever." Hanna had typed, "He's so rude," followed by an angry face, and then, "Can we just do it without him?"

Victoria remembered the last group project, when she'd decided a boy named Marcus was lazy and told everyone so, only to find out he'd been up all nights helping at his family's restaurant. She'd felt awful for weeks afterward. She didn't want to be that person twice. Still, maybe she could infer something from the short replies. Maybe Hassan really didn't care. She typed, deleted, and typed again. Then she sent him a private message: "Are you okay? You sound off today."

The three dots appeared, disappeared, appeared again. Finally: "My grandma had a stroke. She's in the hospital in another city. I can't think about the project."

Victoria sat very still on her bed. So it wasn't Hassan's personality. It was his situation. She remembered Ms. Walker, their teacher, putting a sentence on the board last month: "Psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977." Ms. Walker had said people blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation, then made them find examples in the news. Victoria had written down a homework answer about politicians and forgotten it completely until this moment.

She messaged Hanna. "He's not rude. His grandma is sick. I think we just did that thing Ms. Walker talked about, the fundamental attribution error. Can we split his part until Friday?" Hanna replied with a thumbs up and "I'll take the poster." Victoria offered to write the conclusion section, even though it was the hardest part, and told Hassan not to worry about a single slide.

The next morning Hassan sent the chat a photo from the hospital hallway: his grandmother holding up a shaky thumbs-up sign. "She's talking again," he wrote. Hanna added a row of hearts.

Victoria typed, "Told you the poster looks amazing," because it did, blue and green with real ink, not digital. Hassan answered with the first emoji she'd ever seen him use, a grinning face.

"Fine, one more," he wrote, and sent another one, just to be vain about it.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Burning is a chemical change: wood combines with oxygen and turns into ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour, and it cannot turn back into wood.
story:
Jaxson held the test tube up to the light and frowned. Mr. Cruz had set out five stations in the science lab, and each one had a card that said PHYSICAL or CHEMICAL with the answer hidden under a flap. The rule seemed easy at first: melting ice was physical, because it could freeze back. Rusting was chemical, because it could not be undone. But station four was different. It held a small tin of gray ash, a burnt match, and a card that read: "Can this be un-burned?"

"This one's tricky," said Maximus, leaning over the ash. "Maybe if we heated it again, it would turn back into wood."

"Wood doesn't work that way," Jaxson said slowly, but he wasn't sure why he thought so. Then he remembered the campfire last summer. He and his dad had watched the logs collapse into gray flakes, and Jaxson had asked if they could save the flakes and rebuild a log, the way ice cubes could be melted and refrozen. His dad had just said, "That's gone, buddy. That's gone for good." Jaxson had stared at the smoke curling upward and felt like something had been taken from the world and not returned.

Back in the lab, Daniella flipped open her notebook. "Let's collaborate on this one," she said. "You do the match, I'll do the ash." She touched the ash with a stirring rod, and it crumbled into powder that would never hold the shape of a branch. Jaxson dragged the burnt match across the tray. It left a black smear, not a splinter of pale wood anywhere. Nothing remained that could go back.

"The ice in station two just melted and refroze," Jaxson said. "That was a temporary change, like it was only borrowing the heat. This is different. Something left." He looked at the ash, then at the black smear, and an idea clicked into place like a locker door. "When wood burns, it combines with oxygen. That's why it changes into ash, carbon dioxide, and water vapour. The smoke going up, that's part of the wood leaving."

Daniella scribbled fast. "So it's not just sitting there being burnt. It's turning into new stuff."

"And new stuff can't turn back into wood," Maximus said, peeling the flap on the card. CHEMICAL. He whooped so loudly that a girl at station two dropped her refrozen ice cube, and even from across the room Jaxson could see it shatter and begin, already, to melt.

Mr. Cruz walked over and raised one eyebrow at the tin of ash. "So," he said, tapping the card. "Want to try un-burning it?"

"No way," said Jaxson, pushing the tin toward him. "But if you have any ice, we can un-melt that in about ten minutes."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing 'Deaf' with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase 'deaf' for the hearing condition itself.
story:
Jessica had promised Dahlia the best poster the sign-language club had ever seen, and so far she had produced the word "deaf" in glitter glue, half of it smeared across Dahlia's kitchen table. Dahlia's little brother Marco, who was signing something urgent about snacks, obstructed her view of the marker box by standing right in front of it.

"That's the problem," Dahlia said, tapping the poster. "My brother Nate says it's wrong. Well, he didn't say it, he signed it, then he wrote it down."

Nate's note was still on the counter, and Jessica read it again while Marco stole a cracker. "Look it up," it said. "James Woodward, 1972. He's the reason it matters."

Jessica remembered her own confusion last month at the pharmacy, when she'd been picking up her grandmother's prescription and had seen a flyer for a Deaf community picnic. She'd assumed the capital D was a typo, the kind of extravagant error a poster printer makes at two in the morning. Now she wasn't so sure. She pulled out Dahlia's laptop and typed the name from the note.

"That's it," she said, reading. "In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing Deaf with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase deaf for the hearing condition itself." She looked at Marco, who was signing along with a cartoon. "So when we talk about people, culture, the club, it's the big D."

"Fix the glitter," Dahlia said.

The glitter refused to be fixed, so they flipped the poster over and started fresh on the back. Jessica wrote DEAF CLUB in tall blue letters, then drew hands beneath it, fingers mid-sign. Marco climbed onto a chair to supervise, and when she finished the F he signed the word himself, slow enough for her to copy.

At the door that evening, Dahlia handed her a folded note. "From Nate. He says if the poster looks good, you're in the club whether you like it or not."

Jessica opened it. One word, in careful print, with a very large capital letter: "Deafinitely."

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: A person with anxiety may start avoiding places or activities that worry them, such as school, parties or sports practice.
story:
Piper slid her mom's pharmacy receipt across the counter and waited for the cough syrup, sniffing the air like a detective. The pharmacy smelled like cherry lozenges and floor wax, and the towering shelves of tiny boxes kind of intimidated her, the way a library does when you know exactly one book you need and it is nowhere. That's when she spotted Blake, wedged between the vitamin display and a rack of gummy vitamins, holding a box of bandages like a shield.

Blake was supposed to be home sick. Again. Piper counted on her fingers under the counter: missed Tuesday's practice, Thursday's practice, and Saturday's team party, all with an excuse. Blake had never missed a single practice before, not even the day of the hailstorm, when the whole team had practiced anyway and Coach's umbrella had turned inside out like a frightened bat.

Something clicked, and Piper wanted to test it. She strolled over and held up the cough syrup. "My mom's got the plague. You catching the same thing?"

"Maybe," Blake said, examining the bandage box as if it were fascinating literature. "Probably skipping Monday too. And the swim meet."

"The meet? Blake, you love the meet. You'd swim through a shark tank for the meet." Piper lowered her voice. "And Alivia's birthday is coming, and you already said you might skip that too. That's everything, isn't it? Practice, the party, school stuff."

Blake's shoulders sagged. "It's not like a broken leg. There's nothing to point at."

"I'm not giving you a diagnosis, don't worry," Piper said. "But I'm not leaving you behind the gummy vitamins forever, either." She marched to the counter, where Mr. Gupta, who was also her neighbour and the world's slowest teller of jokes, was boxing up her cough syrup. She leaned in. "Blake's avoiding everything lately. Everything. Who do I tell?"

Mr. Gupta nodded slowly, like she'd brought him a good riddle. "A grown-up Blake trusts. A parent, or the coach. Today would be a fine day."

Piper went back, grabbed Blake's sleeve, and pulled. "Come on. We're telling your mom right now, and on the way you can carry my plague medicine, because my wallet is officially impoverished."

Blake managed half a smile. "You're buying me candy after, though."

"Deal," said Piper. "The good kind, not the vitamin ones."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: According to the USDA, a refrigerator keeps food safely cold for about four hours during a power cut, as long as its door stays closed.
story:
The lights went out at 7:40, right in the middle of Samantha's homework, and the living room went black except for the three candles her mother set on the coffee table. Kenley, who had come over to work on their science project, jumped and then laughed at herself for jumping. They dragged their notebooks to the floor near the candles, but Samantha kept getting up.

"I'm hungry," she said, and walked to the kitchen for the third time. She opened the refrigerator, and the little light inside didn't come on, but the cold air spilled out anyway. She stood in the glow of her phone, moving the milk jug aside, deciding against yogurt, deciding against leftovers, and finally taking a cheese stick. She closed the door. Ten minutes later she was back, opening it again to look for juice.

On her fourth trip her mother called from the couch, "Samantha, stop thwarting the refrigerator."

"What?"

"The fridge keeps food safely cold for about four hours in a power cut," her mother said, "as long as the door stays closed. You keep opening it."

Samantha stood in the dark kitchen holding that. Four hours. The power had been out for maybe forty minutes, so there was plenty of time, but not if she kept letting the cold pour out onto the floor. She thought about it like a bank account with a fixed balance, draining a little every time she peeked. She went back to the living room and found Kenley squinting at a candle flame like it was something sinister.

"New rule," Samantha said. "We decide what we want first, out loud, and then we open the fridge exactly once. One trip for both of us."

"Fine," Kenley said. "Cheese stick and the apple juice."

"Pickle," Samantha said.

They said it over once more, agreed, and walked to the kitchen together. She opened the door, took the juice, the cheese, and the pickle jar, and shut it firmly, letting her hand rest on the warm plastic of the door for a second before turning away.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Like humans, guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C, so they must get it from their food every day.
story:
Antoine had wanted a dog for his whole life, so he still wasn't sure why he'd said yes when Ms. Villanueva held up the guinea pig at the shelter and said, "This one's been waiting a while." Maybe it was the way the animal's whiskers twitched, or maybe it was because his family's apartment had a strict no-dogs rule and twelve years of wanting had taught him to conserve his energy for battles he could actually win. He named her Biscuit and carried the cardboard carrier home through the rain, stopping twice to make sure she was breathing.

For the first week, Biscuit seemed fine. Antoine fed her pellets from the bag Ms. Villanueva had given him, refilled her water bottle, and changed the bedding on Saturdays. Then, on day nine, she stopped moving around her cage. Her fur looked dull, and when he offered a pellet she turned her head away and sat still in the corner, like something heavy was pressing on her.

He called Dev, who knew everything about animals because his cousin worked at a vet clinic. "Pellets and water?" Dev said over the phone. "That's it? Antoine, guinea pigs are like us. They can't make their own vitamin C, so they have to get it from food every single day." Antoine stared at the pellet bag, at the tiny print he'd never read closely, and felt the pieces click together. The pellets were old, maybe the bag had sat at the shelter for months. If the vitamin C had faded out of them, Biscuit had been running on empty all week while he told himself she was just quiet.

He had one variable to change, so he changed it. That night his mom drove him to the grocery store, where he bought a red bell pepper and a bag of parsley, and the cashier raised an eyebrow at the boy buying vegetables and nothing else. Back home, Antoine washed a strip of pepper and held it through the cage bars. Biscuit's nose worked the air. Then her teeth closed around it, and she pulled the whole strip into her paws and began to eat, a small aggressive chomping that Antoine thought was the best sound he'd ever heard.

He sat on the floor beside the cage and texted Dev a photo. Three days later Biscuit was squeaking at him every time the refrigerator opened, loud and demanding, and Antoine was already planning a rotation of peppers and parsley and oranges on a calendar taped to the wall. When his mom asked whether he regretted not getting a dog, he considered it for a moment, watching Biscuit stand up on her hind legs to see whether his hand held anything. "Not even a little," he said, and dropped another strip of pepper into the cage.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Fresh fruits and vegetables are often cheapest at the peak of their local harvest season, when farmers have the most to sell.
story:
Taylor counted her money again, even though the total hadn't changed since breakfast: six dollars and a lint-covered quarter. Last month, strawberries at the farmers' market had cost eight dollars a basket, and she had walked home empty-handed while Mayson ate his in front of her like a raccoon with a treasure chest.

"Six twenty-five," she told Emmie as they passed the honey stall, where a fiddler was playing something that wasn't quite country and wasn't quite folk. "What genre is that supposed to be?" Emmie squinted. "Bee music?" The fiddler winked at them, so at least he had a sense of humor about it.

Taylor's plan had seemed eloquent back in June, back when she'd announced it to her mom: she would buy strawberries, make shortcakes, and sell them at the neighborhood picnic to earn money for art camp. Then she'd seen the price. "Eight dollars," the farmer had said then, "and that's my last basket." Today she was back to try again, and the first thing she noticed was that his table was buried in strawberries. Baskets were stacked three deep, and he kept hauling more crates from a truck behind the stall.

"Four dollars," the farmer said, before she even asked. Taylor blinked. "Each?" He nodded. "Half what I was charging last month." She handed over her money fast, in case he changed his mind, and got two baskets for less than one would have cost in June.

"It doesn't make sense," she said to Emmie, turning the berries over. "Same strawberries. Same farmer. Why would the price just fluctuate like that?" Emmie shrugged, but Taylor kept looking at the table, the crates, the line of customers drifting past toward the tomato stall because tomatoes were everywhere now too. Last month there had been one basket of strawberries at the end of a nearly empty table. Today there were too many to count.

"I think it's about how much he has," Taylor said slowly. "At the peak of strawberry season, when the farmers around here have the most to sell, the price drops. When they barely had any, it was high." She tested it at the next stall, where asparagus, long gone from every other table, cost nine dollars a bunch. The vendor laughed. "Last of it. Want it or not."

"Proof," Taylor whispered, and Emmie groaned. Taylor pointed at her two baskets. "Strawberry shortcake proceeds, art camp, and one eloquent business plan."

"You just like saying eloquent."

"Say it right and it's free," Taylor said, and lifted the baskets toward the bus stop.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so real feeding relationships form a food web of many linked chains rather than one single chain.
story:
Luke crouched beside the garden pond with his sketchbook balanced on one knee, pencil already warm in his hand. Mr. Santos-Reyes had promised the class that whoever drew the clearest feeding chain could help build the new hedgehog house on Saturday, and Luke wanted that job more than anything. He had watched the pond all week, and he knew exactly what he would draw: sun to algae, algae to snail, snail to duck. Four boxes, three arrows, one perfect chain.

"Mine's going to be better than yours," Laurianne whispered, flopping down beside him with her own paper. She smelled like sunscreen and mint gum. "Mr. Santos-Reyes said the chain has to go from the sun all the way to a top predator. Mine ends at a hawk."

"A hawk can't live in a pond," Luke said. "Watch. The duck's the top of mine." He started drawing, confident and quick, and imagined himself steadying the wooden hedgehog panels while Franco held the nails.

Then Laurianne made a strangled sound. "Luke. Look." She pointed at the shallow water near the reeds. The duck had its head down in the weeds, and when it came up, its bill was thick with green pond plants. It gulped them down. A minute later it dipped again and came up with a snail, which vanished with a small, horrible click. Laurianne's pencil hovered over her paper. "It eats both," she said slowly. "It eats the plants and the snails. My chain has the duck eating only snails. That's wrong."

Luke stared at the water, itching to fix his own drawing before it was too late. "So the duck doesn't sit on one line," he said. "It sits on two." He grabbed a fresh sheet and sketched fast: sun, algae, plants, snail, duck, all connected by arrows that branched and crossed. Then he noticed a sparrow hopping along the fence, and a ladybird on a bean stalk, and his arrows multiplied until the page looked like a net with a knot in every corner. "It's not one chain anymore," he said. "It's a web. Lots of chains, all linked."

"That's why the hedgehogs matter," Laurianne said, squinting at the tangled page. "If the snails all vanished, the duck could still eat plants, so it wouldn't just starve." Mr. Santos-Reyes leaned over their shoulders, humming. "Well," he said. "Show me what you've got."

Luke held up his web, messy and crossed out and more coherent than anything he had drawn all year. "A single chain is like a wire," he said, heart pounding. "But a web is like a conductor plate with a hundred paths. If one breaks, the rest can still carry the flow." He paused. "Can we still build the hedgehog house? We'll need to prolong the fence so it can walk in from the field."

Mr. Santos-Reyes grinned and pointed his pen at the pond. "Saturday, eight o'clock. Bring the sketch."

Franco, who had been listening from the compost bins the whole time, cupped his hands around his mouth and shouted, "I call dibs on the nails!"

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, is marked by lighting small oil lamps called diyas and is usually celebrated over five days.
story:
At the temple on Diwali morning, Ivy's grandmother handed her a tray of small clay lamps and pointed at the long window ledge that faced the street. "Line them up before dark," she said, "and leave a gap for one more."

Ivy counted the lamps. Eleven. She set them in a careful row, one at each corner of the ledge first, then filled between them like she did when she set the table, spoons between forks and knives. The gap her grandmother wanted sat right in the middle, and it bothered her. Eleven lamps plus a gap made twelve, which was not a pattern she recognized. She looked down the aisle at the rows of lamps other families had placed along the temple windows, and she counted those too. Ten here, thirteen there, fourteen, eleven. No two rows were the same, and yet every family had left a gap.

"I'm not leaving a hole in the middle," she told her grandmother, ready to rebel against a rule that made no sense. "It looks like somebody dropped one."

Her grandmother laughed and kept folding her sari edge. "They're called diyas," she said, holding one up. "And there are five days of Diwali, so tonight is only the first."

Ivy stood very still. Five days. One lamp for each day. That was the hidden rule, not counting at all. She tested it against the other windows: ten lamps meant a family that had arrived on day one in a past year and come back every year after, and the tallest row, nearly twenty, belonged to the old man by the door who came every single night of every festival since before her mother was born.

She picked up one lamp from her row and set it in the gap, and her grandmother nodded without turning around.

Tomorrow, Ivy decided, she would bring a second diya and place it beside the first. Her row would grow like a parliament passing laws, one vote at a time, until the intricate line of lights stretched the whole width of the ledge and spilled toward the corner where the old man sat, already watching the window and smiling.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: A toothpick pushed into the centre of a muffin that comes out clean or with a few dry crumbs shows the muffin is baked through.
story:
The campsite oven was really just a dented metal box with a flame underneath it, and Bennett had never trusted it. He trusted his dad even less in the morning, before coffee, which was why he had volunteered to bake the blueberry muffins himself. Mr. Chanthavong, the site manager, had handed him a stained recipe card and said, "First thing you do is preheat the oven. It's not a suggestion." Bennett set the dial and decided to allocate the waiting time to reading the card three more times, because last summer he had made pancakes that were raw in the middle and he still hadn't lived it down.

Tenley and David showed up halfway through, drawn by the smell of blueberries someone had stepped on earlier. "Are those going to be done before lunch?" Tenley asked, watching Bennett fold the batter with the concentration of someone defusing a bomb. David sniffed the air. "Hypothetically," he said, "if you burn them, we could still toast marshmallows over the oven flame." Bennett said that was not the backup plan, and cracked an egg.

The timer went off at last, and Bennett opened the oven door. The muffin tops looked pale, almost blond, like they had spent the whole time thinking about turning golden rather than actually doing it. Tenley leaned in and frowned. "They look like they're wearing sunscreen." Bennett stood there holding the timer in one hand. The recipe said thirty minutes, and thirty minutes had passed, so by the recipe's own rules the muffins were done. But his eyes were telling him something different, and his eyes and the recipe card were now in a standoff.

He needed to know what was happening inside the muffins, where he couldn't see, and staring harder wasn't going to help. Then he remembered the toothpick trick, the one his grandmother used without ever announcing it. He pushed a wooden toothpick into the centre of the biggest muffin and pulled it out. The pick came out streaked with wet batter, glistening. He did the same to a second muffin and got the same result, which lowered the probability of the first one being a fluke. "Not done," he announced. "Inside they're still soup." Tenley peered at the toothpick like it was evidence. "So the outside lies?" "The outside is a liar," Bennett said, and slid the tray back in.

Six minutes later he tested again. This time the toothpick came out clean, with only a few dry crumbs clinging to it, and the tops had gone a proper golden brown, as if they'd merely been running late. The muffins tasted warm and buttery, and David ate three of them and claimed a fourth for a hypothetical emergency. Bennett set the last toothpick on the table like a trophy. "Centre of the muffin," he said. "That's the whole trick." Mr. Chanthavong walked by, picked up a muffin, and took a bite. "Bennett," he said, "you may preheat my oven any time."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Research on expert performers has found that how someone practices, focusing on specific weak spots, matters more than simply playing a piece many times.
story:
Alyssa had played "Ode to Joy" eleven times in a row, and she still messed up the same four measures in the middle. The practice room at the community center smelled like floor polish, and her fingers were starting to ache around the clarinet keys. Down the hall, Arwen was waiting for her so they could walk home together.

"You played the whole thing again," Arwen said from the doorway. "The beginning sounded great, though."

"That's the problem," Alyssa said. "The beginning is easy. It's measures twelve through fifteen that fall apart, and I keep playing the easy part over and over instead." She stared at the sheet music, where she had circled the stubborn measures in red pen. She faced a real dilemma: keep practicing the whole song the way she always did, or try something more radical. "I'm only going to play those four measures. Nothing else. Watch."

She set the metronome ticking and played measures twelve through fifteen. She missed the jump to the high E. She played them again. Missed it again, but closer. On the fifth try her fingers finally cooperated, landing on the right keys at the right moment, and she played the four measures clean three times in a row. Then, just to check, she went back to the start and played the entire song from beginning to end.

When she finished, she lowered the clarinet and grinned at Arwen. "I didn't play the whole piece nearly as many times as yesterday, and it sounded better. The four measures aren't the problem anymore."

Arwen clapped from the doorway. "Do that to measure fifteen in my song tomorrow, okay? My mom says I play the whole piece too many times and never fix anything."

"Deal," Alyssa said, and clicked the metronome off.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
