fact: Havdalah, a Hebrew word meaning separation, is the ceremony that ends Shabbat on Saturday night once three stars can be seen in the sky.
story:
Asher's mother had said they would stay at Grandpa Joe's grave until Shabbat was over, which meant no phone, no ride home, and no snacks from the corner store by the gate. Ezekiel had come along because his own Saturday was empty, but now he was hungry and bored, and he kept saying, "Can't you just check the time on your phone? It's in your pocket." That was the problem. Asher couldn't. The day of rest didn't cease just because you were tired of it, and he was trying to keep it the way his family did, all the way through.

"Then when does it end?" Ezekiel asked, kicking a pebble along the path between the headstones.

"When there are three stars," Asher said. "You look up and count them. Then we do Havdalah. That's the word for the ceremony that ends Shabbat, and it means separation, like separating the day of rest from the regular week."

The sky above the cemetery was a stubborn gray, stitched with cloud. Asher tested an idea: maybe stars would appear first where the sky cleared near the horizon, past the tall oak by the fence. He walked to the far corner, gravel crunching under his sneakers, and stood on the low stone border to see over the branches. Ezekiel followed, complaining that his stomach was going to start eating itself, that the new game at the arcade opened at six, and that Asher was acting like the protagonist of some movie where nothing ever happened.

Then a breeze moved through, cold and smelling of cut grass, and the cloud over the oak thinned. One star. Asher held his breath. A second one blinked into the pale patch beside it. He waited, and waited, while Ezekiel counted out loud, "One, two, come on, three." In the branches above, a third point of light showed, small but certain. "There," Asher said. "Three."

They ran back across the grass to where his mother stood with the candle and the little spice box, and Ezekiel, buoyant now that food and the arcade were possible again, shouted, "We saw them first!"

His mother laughed and lit the braided candle. "Then you two get to lead."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: French possessive words agree with the thing owned, not the owner, so "sa mère" can mean either "his mother" or "her mother."
story:
Ethan sat at the kitchen table with his French homework spread out in front of him like a crime scene. The assignment was to describe his family and his cat, Mousse, in full sentences. He had written "J'ai un chat. Mon chat s'appelle Mousse." So far so good. Then he tried to describe his mother, and everything fell apart, because the word for "her mother" and "his mother" looked exactly the same on the page. That couldn't be right. He squinted at "sa mère" for a long moment, wondering if his book had made a printing error, which seemed like the kind of thing that would only happen to him.

He called Charlize on the computer, because Charlize was in French class too and, more importantly, owed him a favor for the sandwich incident. Charlize answered with her own agenda. "Before anything else, tell me if Mousse is available for my video," she said. "He has to sit on my shoulder like an entrepreneur's parrot. It's for a project where I show how my cat-sitting business will thrive." Ethan said he would consider it, which meant no.

"Read me your sentences," Charlize said. "I'll draw the family you describe. If I draw it right, your French works." It was an approximate test, but it was a test, which was more than the textbook offered. Ethan read out, "J'ai un frère. Il a une mère. Sa mère est grande." Charlize drew a boy and a brother, and then stopped. "Whose mother? His mother or your mother? It says the same thing for both. I can't tell unless you tell me."

Ethan looked at "sa mère" again. So that was the trick. The word matched the mother, not the person who owned the mother, which meant every listener in France was walking around asking follow-up questions. He grinned and read the sentence again, slower this time, watching Charlize hold her pencil over two possible drawings. "Guess," he said. She guessed the brother's mother. "Wrong," said Ethan. "That's my mom. Want to try again?" Charlize put down her pencil. "First we negotiate the parrot."

activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
knowledge_domain: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
fact: Where contour lines are packed close together the ground is steep; where they are spread far apart the slope is gentle.
story:
The paper map crackled on the dashboard as Hailey traced the brown squiggles with one finger. Three hours into the road trip, her dad had handed it back to her and said the GPS was acting obsolete, useless, like a toaster that only made one piece of toast. So the map was in charge now, and Hailey was in charge of the map.

"Pick a trail up Sugarloaf Hill," Eileen said from the middle seat, chin hooked over Hailey's shoulder. "Phoebe wants the hard one."

"I want the interesting one," Phoebe corrected. She jabbed a fingertip at the western side of the hill. "This one. Look how many lines it crosses. More lines, more work, more glory."

Hailey squinted. On Phoebe's route, the brown lines were jammed together like the stripes on a candy cane. On the eastern trail, the same lines drifted apart, wide and lazy, like ripples spreading in a pond. She remembered a girl at summer camp pointing at a map exactly like this one and saying, "Where they're packed close, it's steep; where they're spread out, it's gentle." Hailey had believed her, and now she wanted to test it.

"That's a contradiction," Hailey said slowly. "You want the hard trail, but your trail might be the brutal one. The lines on your side are squished together. That means steep. The other side is gentle, because they're spread apart."

Phoebe frowned at the paper like it had insulted her. "It's just lines."

"Lines don't lie," Hailey said. "Let's take the gentle one, and if I'm wrong, you can say so the whole way up."

"Deal," said Phoebe. "And I'll be very thorough about it."

They parked at the eastern trailhead, and the girls started up a path that rose in long, easy ramps through pine shade that smelled like resin and cool dirt. Phoebe huffed once, waited, then admitted nothing. Halfway up, she stopped, pulled a granola bar from her pocket, and broke it in two.

"Fine," she said, handing half to Hailey. "Steep can wait for next year."

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: Latitude measures how far north or south a place is from the equator, from 0 degrees at the equator to 90 degrees at each pole.
story:
Arianna spread the giant atlas across the kitchen table, which was really the living room table pretending to be a kitchen table, since their apartment had one table and everyone took turns with it. Ms. Sutherland from downstairs had brought up a stack of postcards from her travels and promised a chocolate bar to whoever guessed which of her cities sat closest to the equator. Arianna intended to win that chocolate bar with science.

Kendrick arrived with his own theory. "It's got to be Moscow," he said, tapping the list. "It's huge. Big cities are warm, right? People everywhere." Arianna had to confess that her own first guess had been something similar, that the numbers on the map's side lines were like scores, and the biggest number meant the winner. She had picked a city way up at 60 because 60 beat 23.

Then she noticed the map's fine print and traced the line labeled 0 across the middle of the world. "Latitude," she read aloud. Kendrick leaned in. "It's how far north or south a place is from the equator. Zero at the equator, ninety at each pole." She checked it against the globe in the corner, spinning it until the fat middle line faced her. The equator wasn't a score at all. It was the starting line, and the higher the number, the farther you'd walked away from it toward a pole.

"So a small number means close," Kendrick said slowly, like he was tasting the idea. "And sixty isn't close. Sixty is practically a penguin." He crossed out Moscow himself, which Arianna thought was generous of him, since he had defended Moscow for a full ten minutes. They worked down the list together, hunting each city and reading its number aloud. Singapore sat at about one degree. One. Practically on the starting line.

Arianna felt a small, private wobble as she wrote her answer, the way she felt standing on the top step of a ladder, slightly vulnerable and very aware of it, because she had been confidently wrong once already today. Still, one was less than twenty-three, and less than sixty, and numbers did not lie even when cities were huge and full of people wearing shorts.

They took the answer down to Ms. Sutherland's door and knocked. She opened it holding a kettle and raised one eyebrow at their piece of paper. "Singapore," Arianna said. "Latitude one degree north." Ms. Sutherland set the kettle down and reached toward the top of the fridge.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: British economist Alfred Marshall popularized the supply-and-demand diagram, with its two crossing curves, in his 1890 book Principles of Economics.
story:
Luke taped the last paper cup to the table and stared at his poster. It showed two crooked lines crossing like an X, and above it, in marker, "SUPPLY AND DEMAND: A Lemonade Report." Homework for Mr. Morningstar, due tomorrow, worth half his science-ish grade, whatever that meant.

"Your poster looks like a spider got squashed," said Marius, who had contributed three lemons, one box of sugar, and an hour of complaining.

"They're curves. Supply goes up, demand goes down, they cross. Strawberries cost two dollars in summer and five in winter. That's the whole thing. I just don't know who invented the squashed-spider part."

"Charge the customers extra and find out," Marius said, because Marius wanted one thing only: enough money for the new soccer cards at the shop, which closed at four o'clock. It was already two.

Their first customer was Ahmad, who read the poster while Luke poured. "Who drew the first one of these X things?"

"Nobody knows," Luke said, sweating. "Maybe a wizard."

Ahmad paid a dollar and drank. "Mr. Morningstar loves questions like that. You should look it up."

At the picnic table, Luke thumbed through the class textbook and found, in a corner, a small boxed note. His eyes went wide. "Marius! It says here a British economist, Alfred Marshall, made these crossing curves famous in his 1890 book, Principles of Economics!"

"Add it before you forget," Marius said, counting quarters.

Luke wrote it in marker, careful and consistent with his neatest letters. Then he tested his idea out loud on the next customer, a woman with a dog. "See, in summer there are tons of strawberries, so they're cheap. In winter, hardly any, so they're dear."

"Smart boy," she said, buying two cups. "My dog likes strawberries too, poor thing, he can't have them." Luke felt a stab of empathy for the dog and tossed him a dog biscuit from his pocket.

By 3:40 they had eleven dollars. Marius sprinted for the card shop, cards flapping, and Luke ran after him, poster under his arm.

"Marshall!" Luke shouted down the street. "1890!"

"Run faster!" Marius shouted back.

activity: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
knowledge_domain: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
fact: In 410 CE, the Visigoths led by Alaric captured and sacked the city of Rome, the first time in about 800 years that a foreign enemy had taken it.
story:
Carter spread the photocopied map across the archive table and weighted the corners with reference books nobody was allowed to borrow. Mr. Barrett, the archivist, had warned him that the reading room closed at four, which gave Carter exactly fifty minutes to figure out his history project: explaining, with borders, why the Roman Empire split and fell.

Journey leaned over the map, tapping the thick line that split the empire down the middle. "I thought Rome fell in one big crash," she said. "This looks more like it just got cut in half."

"That's the split," Carter said. "Two halves, east and west. The west is the part that fell apart." He traced the western border with his finger, and that was where the problem started. The border looked huge, wrapped around like a stretched rubber band, and he could not see how a line on paper could tell him anything about an empire dying. He needed proof he could actually point to, not just a paragraph copied from a website.

"Try the dates box," Journey said. Carter pulled the folder of timeline cards Mr. Barrett had left beside the map. One card stopped him cold. In 410 CE, the Visigoths, led by a king named Alaric, captured the city of Rome and sacked it. Journey read over his shoulder. "Wait. Rome itself got captured? I thought that happened at the very end."

"That's what I thought too," Carter said slowly. "But this says it was the first time in about 800 years that a foreign enemy had taken the city." He set the card on the map, right on the dot marked Rome, far inside the border. The border had not moved at all, and the enemy was standing in the middle of the empire anyway. The line was not the wall he had imagined. It was more like a fence with the gate hanging open.

"So your whole project is wrong?" Journey asked.

"No," Carter said, and he flipped his notebook to a fresh page. "It's better. The borders show where Rome stopped being able to protect what was inside them." He began copying the map, drawing arrows from the border toward the city. "Help me with the arrows. Mr. Barrett says we can have fifteen more minutes if we're actually writing."

Mr. Barrett glanced over from the front desk, saw the arrows marching across the page, and turned the clock toward the wall without a word.

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: In a two-part choir of higher voices, the upper part is usually called soprano and the lower part alto.
story:
Nolan had been coming to Grandpa's house every Thursday since school let out, because Grandpa's church choir needed boys' voices and Grandpa had promised the director a grandson who could carry a tune. What nobody had promised was that Nolan would be handed the lower part on the very first night. The director, a small woman with a pencil behind her ear, pointed at his sheet and said, "Alto." He stared at the word like it was a punishment.

Braeden, who had joined with him, leaned over during the water break. "You got the low one? I got soprano. That's the real tune." His grin said everything his voice didn't. Braeden had wanted the top part since the first rehearsal, and he'd been practicing it in the locker room, showing off the high notes to anyone who would listen.

At Grandpa's kitchen table afterward, Nolan spread both sheets side by side. The soprano line carried the melody everyone would recognize, but when he followed his own line with his finger, he noticed it wasn't just a shadow of Braeden's. It bent away on purpose, dipped where Braeden soared, and when the two lines crossed, something happened in the air that neither could make alone. He hummed his part against the recording Grandpa put on, and it felt like the two metals in Grandpa's old ring, an alloy, stronger blended than either was by itself.

Grandpa slid a letter across the table, one Nolan's great-aunt had written years ago when she'd sung in the same choir. "They tried to make me sing the melody," she'd written, "but I held the low line all through the war years, and the choir never sounded so full. The lower part isn't trivial, whatever the tenors say. It governs where the harmony can go." Nolan read it twice.

The next Thursday, when Braeden smirked and said, "Still stuck on the leftover notes?", Nolan shrugged. "Soprano just means the higher voices," he said. "Alto's the lower. That's all it means." At rehearsal they stood the two parts shoulder to shoulder, and when the chord locked, Braeden stopped smirking and just listened.

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: In the United States, calling or texting 988 reaches the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which began on July 16, 2022.
story:
The pharmacy smelled like hand sanitizer and cough drops, and Emma was supposed to be picking up her little brother's medicine while her mom waited in the car. She found Nate standing in the aisle of bandages, staring at a box of gauze like it was written in a foreign language. His hands were shaking. That was the third strange thing she'd noticed that week: Monday he'd skipped lunch, Tuesday he'd snapped at Santiago over nothing, and now this.

"Nate, you okay?" she asked.

"I'm fine," he said, but his voice came out defiant, like he was daring her to believe him. He put the box down and picked it up again, twice.

Emma followed him toward the front of the store, thinking hard. She couldn't see what was wrong inside him, but she could see the clues, and she could deduce the rest. A pattern, her science teacher would call it. When a pattern pointed to someone hurting, you didn't ignore it. Her mom had told her once that noticing was the foundation of being a good friend, and she was starting to understand what that meant.

Then she saw the poster by the register, blue and white, next to the blood pressure machine. It said that calling or texting 988 reaches the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which began on July 16, 2022, in the United States. She read it twice. She hadn't known that before. She memorized it anyway, because Nate's hands were still shaking and she wanted something to hold on to.

Mr. Luo, who ran the pharmacy counter, leaned over and said quietly, "Everything all right with your friend?"

Emma looked at Nate, then back at Mr. Luo. "I don't think so," she said. "Can you help?"

Mr. Luo came around the counter and set a stool down beside the blood pressure machine. "Sit with me a minute, Nate," he said, and Emma texted her mom: found Nate, staying with him. Nate sat. His hands went still.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: In 1714 the British Parliament offered a prize of up to 20,000 pounds for a practical way to find a ship's longitude at sea.
story:
Ava pressed her nose against the window of Travel Time Tours, where a giant world map covered the back wall with thin lines crossing it like graph paper. Her mother had delegated the job of planning the family trip to her, all because Ava had once memorized every capital in Europe, and now she stood in the doorway clutching a notebook and a granola bar.

"I need to find Quito," she told Ms. Bouchard, the agent behind the counter. "It's in Ecuador. But it's a tiny dot on your map."

Ms. Bouchard smiled and spun the big globe beside her desk. "Then you'll want to learn its address. Latitude first, then longitude." She tapped the lines running sideways around the globe. "Find the equator. Count up."

Ava traced her finger north from the fat middle line, feeling the cool lacquer under her fingertip. "About a pinky-width above the equator," she said slowly. "So zero degrees latitude, then north a little. That's the sideways part." Then she followed a line from pole to pole. "And the up-and-down lines meet it there. So Quito has an address, like a house." She checked the index of the atlas on the counter. S0.23, W78.5. Close enough to her finger. She grinned so wide her granola bar nearly slipped.

"Why are the sideways ones easier, though?" asked Brantley, who had tagged along for the free pamphlets. "In school we read that in 1714 the British Parliament offered a prize of up to 20,000 pounds for a practical way to find a ship's longitude at sea. Twenty thousand pounds! Just for the up-and-down lines!"

Ava turned the globe, watching the lines bend away from her. "Latitude, you can get from the sun and stars, I think. But longitude at sea must have been like being blindfolded in a hallway with no numbers on the doors." She spun the globe and stopped it with one finger. "Buenos Aires. Let's find its address before Mom gets here." Brantley leaned in, and together they started counting.

The fire station smelled like rubber boots and old coffee, and Charlie stood with her class in front of a gleaming red engine while Mr. Fernando, the station's oldest firefighter, talked about the alarm system. Behind him, half hidden in shadows, sat a scarred wooden desk that looked older than everything else in the room combined. Charlie wanted to know why. She raised her hand. "What's that desk for?"

Mr. Fernando smiled. "That desk belonged to the station's first chief, back in 1912. Every logbook from a hundred years of fires was written on it." The class moved on toward the pole, but Charlie hung back, and so did Drayden, who was already drifting toward the desk with his hand out, fingers inches from the dark wood.

"Stop," Charlie said, grabbing his sleeve. Wyatt turned around too. "Remember the museum? They told us why you can't touch things." Wyatt nodded. "Oils and salts from your skin build up over time," he recited. "They stain and damage the surfaces. That's why so many museums ask visitors not to touch anything."

Drayden looked at his own hand like it had betrayed him. "Just once, though?"

"One time is never one time," Charlie said. She was thinking about the brass rail on the pole, which firefighters gripped every single day. It was worn smooth and pale in a hand-shaped band, and the desk, which nobody was supposed to touch, still kept its dark finish after a century. She pointed at the rail, then at the desk. "Look. The rail gets touched constantly, and it's changed colour. The desk doesn't get touched, and it hasn't. That's the pattern. Your hand would leave the same stuff behind, just slower."

Mr. Fernando had drifted back and was listening with his arms crossed. "That's the most credible theory I've heard from a field trip all year," he said. "You three want to excavate the old file cabinet next to it? There might be a letter in there nobody's read since I started here." They found one, yellow and crisp, from a chief to his crew, dated decades back. Charlie read it aloud by the window.

"To whoever finds this," it began. "The desk came with me from the old harbour station. It has been through two floods and one very determined pigeon. Please keep hands, coffee cups, and pigeons off it. It has earned its rest." Drayden put both hands firmly in his pockets, and Wyatt laughed so hard the letter rattled. Charlie smoothed the page flat on the cabinet, not the desk, and read the last line again.
